title: Identity & Belonging
subtitle: Talk about where you come from, living abroad, and how to nuance stereotypes

lessons.title: D'où je viens
lessons.description: Describe your origins, the place where you grew up and what shaped the person you are today.

blocks.heading: Saying where you come from
blocks.body: French has several ways to place yourself geographically, and they are not interchangeable. «Je viens de» is the most neutral. «Je suis originaire de» sounds slightly more formal and points at family roots rather than your last address. «J'ai grandi à» separates where you were born from where you actually grew up — a useful distinction when the two are different.

examples.french: Je viens d'une petite ville du sud-ouest.
examples.english: I come from a small town in the south-west.

examples.french: Je suis originaire de Lyon, mais je n'y habite plus.
examples.english: I'm originally from Lyon, but I don't live there any more.

examples.french: Je suis né à Dakar et j'ai grandi à Nantes.
examples.english: I was born in Dakar and I grew up in Nantes.

examples.french: Mes parents viennent de deux régions très différentes.
examples.english: My parents come from two very different regions.

examples.french: Ma ville natale est au bord de la mer.
examples.english: My home town is by the sea.

blocks.tip: «D'où tu viens ?» can sound abrupt to someone who has heard it too often. «Tu as grandi où ?» is warmer and invites a story rather than a label.

blocks.heading: Painting the place you grew up in
blocks.body: To describe a childhood setting, French uses the imparfait: it sets a background, a habit, an atmosphere. Add sensory detail and the description immediately sounds like a real memory rather than a form you are filling in.

examples.french: C'était un quartier tranquille où tout le monde se connaissait.
examples.english: It was a quiet neighbourhood where everybody knew each other.

examples.french: Il y avait un marché tous les samedis matin.
examples.english: There was a market every Saturday morning.

examples.french: On passait nos étés à la campagne, chez ma grand-mère.
examples.english: We used to spend our summers in the countryside, at my grandmother's.

examples.french: La maison sentait toujours le pain grillé.
examples.english: The house always smelled of toast.

examples.french: Je m'ennuyais un peu, mais je m'y sentais en sécurité.
examples.english: I was a little bored there, but I felt safe.

blocks.tip: «Chez ma grand-mère», «chez mes parents» — chez + person is far more natural than «à la maison de…».

blocks.heading: Saying what shaped you
blocks.body: Beyond geography, identity is about what was passed on to you: a language, a job, a set of values, a way of arguing at the dinner table. Verbs like marquer, façonner, transmettre and the expression «ce qui m'a marqué, c'est…» let you talk about influence without sounding like a textbook.

examples.french: Ce qui m'a le plus marqué, c'est le silence de la campagne.
examples.english: What marked me most is the silence of the countryside.

examples.french: Mes grands-parents m'ont transmis leur langue.
examples.english: My grandparents passed their language on to me.

examples.french: Ce milieu m'a façonné plus que je ne le pensais.
examples.english: That environment shaped me more than I thought.

examples.french: J'ai hérité de son caractère têtu.
examples.english: I inherited his stubborn character.

examples.french: Je ne me sens pas d'un seul endroit, et ça me va.
examples.english: I don't feel I'm from a single place, and that's fine with me.

blocks.tip: «Ce qui… c'est…» is a very common way to highlight one idea: «Ce qui compte, c'est la famille.» Keep the c'est — French rarely drops it.

blocks.heading: Relative pronouns: qui, que, où, dont
blocks.body: Talking about origins means linking a place or a person to extra information, and that is exactly what relative pronouns do. Use qui when the relative is the subject of the next verb, que when it is the object, où for a place or a moment in time, and dont when the verb or noun that follows needs de (parler de, se souvenir de, avoir besoin de, le fils de…).

examples.french: C'est un village qui compte moins de trois cents habitants.
examples.english: It's a village that has fewer than three hundred inhabitants.

examples.french: Les valeurs que mes parents m'ont transmises sont simples.
examples.english: The values my parents passed on to me are simple.

examples.french: La rue où j'ai grandi n'existe plus.
examples.english: The street where I grew up no longer exists.

examples.french: C'est une période dont je me souviens très bien.
examples.english: It's a period I remember very well.

examples.french: L'année où on est partis, j'avais douze ans.
examples.english: The year we left, I was twelve.

blocks.tip: Quick test: replace the relative with a full sentence. «Je me souviens DE cette période» → de is there, so dont. «J'ai vu cette période» → no de, so que.

blocks.heading: Imparfait or passé composé in a childhood story
blocks.body: When you narrate where you come from, both tenses appear in the same paragraph. The imparfait gives the setting and repeated habits — how things generally were. The passé composé gives the events that moved the story forward: the move, the birth, the day everything changed. Beginners tend to over-use the passé composé; a good origin story is mostly imparfait with a few sharp passé composé sentences.

examples.french: On habitait au troisième étage et il n'y avait pas d'ascenseur.
examples.english: We lived on the third floor and there was no lift.

examples.french: Un jour, mon père a trouvé un travail à l'étranger.
examples.english: One day, my father found a job abroad.

examples.french: Je jouais dans la cour quand ils me l'ont annoncé.
examples.english: I was playing in the courtyard when they told me.

examples.french: Chaque été, on retournait au village.
examples.english: Every summer, we went back to the village.

examples.french: En 2010, on a quitté la région pour de bon.
examples.english: In 2010, we left the region for good.

blocks.tip: Time markers help you choose: chaque été, souvent, tous les jours, à l'époque → imparfait. Un jour, soudain, en 2010, deux fois → passé composé.

items.prompt: Introduce where your family comes from.
items.tip: In «originaire», the g is soft: o-ree-ZHEE-nair. Don't stress the last syllable too hard — French keeps a flat, even rhythm.

items.tip: «se connaissait» ends in -ait: say -EH, not -ay. Link «tout le monde» smoothly: too-luh-MOND.

items.tip: «plus» before a consonant sound keeps its s silent: play-plü-fa-so-NAY. Keep «c'est» short and unstressed.

passages.title: La maison de Nadia
passages.french:
Quand on me demande d'où je viens, je ne sais jamais quoi répondre en une phrase.
Je suis née à Rennes, mais mes parents venaient d'ailleurs et on a déménagé quatre fois avant mes douze ans.
La maison dont je me souviens le mieux, c'est celle de ma grand-mère, en Bretagne.
Il y avait un jardin en pente, un cerisier, et une cuisine qui sentait toujours quelque chose de sucré.
Chaque été, on y retournait pour trois semaines.
Ma grand-mère nous parlait dans une langue que je comprenais sans savoir la parler.
À l'école, personne ne connaissait cette langue, alors je n'en parlais pas.
J'avais un peu honte, je crois, et aujourd'hui ça me semble absurde.
À trente ans, j'ai commencé à prendre des cours pour la réapprendre.
Mon accent fait rire mes cousins, mais ma grand-mère, elle, ne rit pas.
Elle corrige, elle répète, elle attend.
Je ne viens pas d'un seul endroit, et j'ai fini par accepter cette réponse compliquée.
passages.english:
When people ask me where I'm from, I never know how to answer in one sentence.
I was born in Rennes, but my parents came from elsewhere and we moved four times before I turned twelve.
The house I remember best is my grandmother's, in Brittany.
There was a sloping garden, a cherry tree, and a kitchen that always smelled of something sweet.
Every summer, we went back there for three weeks.
My grandmother spoke to us in a language I understood without being able to speak it.
At school, nobody knew that language, so I didn't mention it.
I was a little ashamed, I think, and today that seems absurd to me.
At thirty, I started taking classes to learn it again.
My accent makes my cousins laugh, but my grandmother doesn't laugh.
She corrects, she repeats, she waits.
I don't come from a single place, and I've ended up accepting that complicated answer.

lessons.title: Vivre à l'étranger
lessons.description: Talk about settling in another country: adapting, culture shock, what you miss and what you gain.

blocks.heading: Arriving and settling in
blocks.body: Moving abroad has its own vocabulary in French. «S'installer» is the key verb: it covers arriving, finding a flat and starting a life. «Vivre à l'étranger» is the general state; «partir à l'étranger» is the decision. Note that «l'étranger» means both abroad and a foreigner — the article and preposition tell you which.

examples.french: Je me suis installé à Bruxelles il y a trois ans.
examples.english: I settled in Brussels three years ago.

examples.french: Au début, tout me paraissait compliqué : la banque, le loyer, les papiers.
examples.english: At first everything seemed complicated to me: the bank, the rent, the paperwork.

examples.french: Les démarches administratives m'ont pris six mois.
examples.english: The administrative procedures took me six months.

examples.french: J'ai mis longtemps à trouver un logement correct.
examples.english: It took me a long time to find a decent place to live.

examples.french: Ce n'était pas un choix définitif, au départ.
examples.english: It wasn't a permanent choice, at the start.

blocks.tip: «Mettre du temps à + infinitif» is the natural way to say something took you a while: «J'ai mis six mois à comprendre l'humour local.»

blocks.heading: Culture shock and adapting
blocks.body: Le choc culturel rarely comes from big things; it comes from small ones — how people queue, how directly they say no, what time dinner happens. French speakers describe this with s'adapter, s'habituer à, le décalage and le dépaysement. Note that «s'habituer» always takes à: on s'habitue à quelque chose.

examples.french: Le choc culturel n'est pas venu tout de suite.
examples.english: The culture shock didn't come straight away.

examples.french: Je me suis habitué aux horaires, mais pas au climat.
examples.english: I got used to the schedule, but not to the climate.

examples.french: Il y a un décalage entre ce que j'imaginais et la réalité.
examples.english: There's a gap between what I imagined and reality.

examples.french: Au bout d'un an, j'ai commencé à me sentir chez moi.
examples.english: After a year, I started to feel at home.

examples.french: La barrière de la langue a été le plus dur.
examples.english: The language barrier was the hardest part.

blocks.tip: «Au bout de + durée» = after a period of time, seen from inside the experience. «Après un an» is neutral; «au bout d'un an» suggests you waited.

blocks.heading: What you miss, what you gain
blocks.body: Two structures do most of the work here. «Quelque chose me manque» is inverted compared to English: the thing missed is the subject. And to weigh gains against losses, French speakers reach for «en revanche», «malgré tout», «ce que j'ai gagné, c'est…».

examples.french: Ma famille me manque, surtout le dimanche.
examples.english: I miss my family, especially on Sundays.
examples.note: literally: my family is missing to me

examples.french: Ce qui me manque le plus, c'est le bruit du marché.
examples.english: What I miss most is the noise of the market.

examples.french: En revanche, j'ai gagné en indépendance.
examples.english: On the other hand, I've gained in independence.

examples.french: Malgré la solitude, je ne regrette rien.
examples.english: Despite the loneliness, I regret nothing.

examples.french: L'expérience a été difficile mais enrichissante.
examples.english: The experience was difficult but enriching.

blocks.tip: Never say «Je manque ma famille» — that means you are absent. It is «Ma famille me manque» / «Tu me manques».

blocks.heading: The verb manquer — backwards from English
blocks.body: In French, the thing you miss is the subject and the person who misses it is an indirect object pronoun (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur). So «I miss Paris» becomes «Paris me manque» — Paris is missing to me. The verb agrees with what is missed, not with the person: «Mes amis me manquent» (plural verb).

examples.french: Tu me manques.
examples.english: I miss you.
examples.note: not «Je te manque», which means you miss me

examples.french: Mes amis me manquent le week-end.
examples.english: I miss my friends at the weekend.

examples.french: Est-ce que la France te manque ?

blocks.heading: Saying how long: depuis, il y a, ça fait… que, pendant
blocks.body: Expat stories are full of durations, and French splits them carefully. Depuis + a length or a starting point, with the PRESENT tense, for something still going on. Il y a + a length points at a finished moment in the past. «Ça fait … que» is the spoken equivalent of depuis. Pendant covers a completed stretch of time.

passages.title: Deux ans plus tard
passages.french:
Quand je suis arrivé, je pensais que le plus dur serait la langue.
En réalité, c'était le silence du dimanche.
Chez moi, le dimanche, il y avait du bruit, des voisins, une table trop pleine.
Ici, tout le monde reste chez soi et la ville se repose.
Pendant six mois, j'ai gardé mes habitudes d'avant, comme si j'allais repartir.
Je n'avais pas accroché de photos, je n'avais pas acheté de vraie casserole.
Et puis un collègue m'a invité à dîner, sans raison particulière.
On a parlé quatre heures et je suis rentré à pied, tard.
Ce soir-là, j'ai compris que je pouvais construire quelque chose ici.
Aujourd'hui, ma famille me manque toujours, surtout quand quelqu'un tombe malade.
En revanche, j'ai gagné une liberté que je n'avais pas avant.
Je ne sais pas si je resterai, mais je ne vis plus avec ma valise ouverte.
passages.english:
When I arrived, I thought the hardest thing would be the language.
In reality, it was the silence of Sundays.
Back home, on Sundays there was noise, neighbours, an overcrowded table.
Here, everyone stays at home and the city rests.
For six months, I kept my old habits, as if I were about to leave again.
I hadn't hung up any photos, I hadn't bought a real saucepan.
And then a colleague invited me to dinner, for no particular reason.
We talked for four hours and I walked home, late.
That evening, I understood that I could build something here.
Today, I still miss my family, especially when someone falls ill.
On the other hand, I've gained a freedom I didn't have before.
I don't know whether I'll stay, but I no longer live with my suitcase open.

lessons.title: Les préjugés
lessons.description: Learn to recognise a generalisation, question it politely, and replace it with something more accurate.

blocks.heading: Spotting a generalisation in the grammar itself
blocks.body: A generalisation is often visible before you even judge the content: it uses a plural group as subject with no qualifier — «les X sont…», «ils font tous…», «chez eux, c'est toujours…». The grammar turns millions of individuals into one block. Learning to hear that shape is the first skill of this lesson; you will practise replacing it, not repeating it.

examples.french: « Ils sont tous comme ça. » — c'est une généralisation.
examples.english: "They're all like that." — that's a generalisation.

examples.french: Le mot « tous » devrait déjà nous alerter.
examples.english: The word "all" should already alert us.

examples.french: Une phrase sans exception, c'est rarement une phrase vraie.
examples.english: A sentence with no exceptions is rarely a true sentence.

examples.french: On parle d'un groupe entier à partir de deux rencontres.
examples.english: We talk about a whole group on the basis of two encounters.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas une observation, c'est un raccourci.
examples.english: That's not an observation, it's a mental shortcut.

blocks.tip: Test any sentence by adding «sans exception» at the end. If it suddenly sounds absurd, it was a generalisation.

blocks.heading: Language that puts the individual back
blocks.body: The repair is usually grammatical too. Replace the group subject with a person: «une personne que j'ai rencontrée», «mon voisin», «elle». Replace the eternal present with a dated experience: «ce jour-là», «dans cette entreprise». Add a qualifier: certains, parfois, dans mon expérience.

examples.french: Plutôt que « les gens d'ici », dis « les collègues de mon bureau ».
examples.english: Rather than "people here", say "my colleagues at the office".

examples.french: Dans mon expérience, ça s'est passé comme ça une fois.
examples.english: In my experience, it happened that way once.

examples.french: Certaines personnes, oui ; toutes, sûrement pas.
examples.english: Some people, yes; all of them, certainly not.

examples.french: Je ne parle que de ce que j'ai vu moi-même.
examples.english: I'm only talking about what I saw myself.

examples.french: C'est vrai pour lui, mais je n'en tire pas de règle.
examples.english: It's true of him, but I don't draw a rule from it.

blocks.tip: «Je ne… que» means only, not a negative: «Je ne parle que de mon cas» = I'm only talking about my case.

blocks.heading: Disagreeing without a fight
blocks.body: You will sometimes want to push back on an idée reçue in conversation. French offers softeners that keep the exchange friendly: «je ne suis pas sûr que…», «ça dépend beaucoup», «j'ai plutôt l'impression que…», «tu as un exemple précis ?». Asking for a concrete example is often more effective than contradicting.

examples.english: I'm not sure it's that simple.

blocks.tip: «Nuancer» is a compliment in French: «une réponse nuancée» is a thoughtful one, not a wishy-washy one.

blocks.heading: The subjunctive of doubt: je ne pense pas que…
blocks.body: When you express doubt or deny a certainty, the verb that follows que goes into the subjunctive. Compare «Je pense que c'est vrai» (indicative — you're sure) with «Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai» (subjunctive — you're not). This is the politest tool in the lesson: it lets you disagree without declaring the other person wrong. The common irregular forms are soit (être), ait (avoir), fasse (faire), puisse (pouvoir), aille (aller).

examples.french: Je ne pense pas que ce soit aussi général.
examples.english: I don't think it's that general.

examples.french: Je ne crois pas qu'on puisse dire ça de tout un pays.
examples.english: I don't think you can say that about a whole country.

examples.french: Il est possible qu'elle ait eu une mauvaise expérience.
examples.english: It's possible she had a bad experience.

examples.french: Je doute que deux exemples suffisent.
examples.english: I doubt two examples are enough.

examples.french: Bien que ce soit courant, ce n'est pas vrai partout.
examples.english: Although it's common, it isn't true everywhere.
examples.note: bien que always takes the subjunctive

blocks.tip: Positive certainty keeps the indicative: «Je suis sûr que c'est vrai.» Only doubt, negation and expressions like il faut que trigger the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: Quantifiers that stop a sentence generalising
blocks.body: The difference between a fair observation and a prejudice is often one small word. Certains (some), quelques-uns (a few), la plupart (most), un certain nombre de (a number of) all narrow a claim honestly. Note the agreement: certaines personnes, la plupart des gens pensent (plural verb after la plupart des).

examples.french: Certaines personnes réagissent comme ça, d'autres non.
examples.english: Some people react like that, others don't.

examples.french: La plupart des étudiants que j'ai rencontrés étaient stressés.

examples.french: Quelques-uns de mes collègues pensent l'inverse.

examples.french: Ça arrive parfois, ce n'est pas une règle.
examples.english: It happens sometimes, it isn't a rule.

blocks.tip: Swap «toujours» for «souvent» and «tous» for «certains» and most sweeping statements become defensible — and more interesting.

passages.title: La question de trop
passages.french:
Camille travaille depuis six mois dans une petite librairie.
Un client lui a demandé un jour d'où elle venait « vraiment ».
Elle a répondu : « De la rue d'à côté. »
Il a insisté, gentiment, sans se rendre compte qu'il posait la question pour la centième fois.
Ce n'était pas de la méchanceté, c'était une habitude.
Camille dit qu'elle ne s'énerve plus ; elle propose autre chose.
Elle demande au client ce qu'il lit en ce moment, et la conversation repart ailleurs.
« Les gens ne veulent pas me réduire, dit-elle, ils vont simplement au plus court. »
Son collègue Malik, lui, préfère répondre franchement que la question le fatigue.
Les deux ont raison, et ils n'ont pas la même patience le même jour.
Ce que Camille demande n'est pas compliqué : une question, pas une catégorie.
Et si on se trompe, dit-elle, il suffit d'écouter la réponse jusqu'au bout.
passages.english:
Camille has been working in a small bookshop for six months.
One day a customer asked her where she was "really" from.
She replied: "From the street next door."
He insisted, kindly, without realising he was asking the question for the hundredth time.
It wasn't malice, it was a habit.
Camille says she no longer gets annoyed; she offers something else instead.
She asks the customer what he's reading at the moment, and the conversation moves elsewhere.
"People don't want to reduce me," she says, "they just take the shortest route."
Her colleague Malik, for his part, prefers to say frankly that the question tires him.
Both are right, and they don't have the same patience on the same day.
What Camille asks for isn't complicated: a question, not a category.
And if you get it wrong, she says, you just have to listen to the answer all the way through.
